newsitem.title: UK: SOCCER-CELTIC ROCKED BY DOUBLE DOSE OF BAD NEWS.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-CELTIC ROCKED BY DOUBLE DOSE OF BAD NEWS.

text.p: Celtic's sorry season continued on Friday with a public row between Italian striker Paolo Di Canio and owner Fergus McCann and the news that stalwart midfielder Paul McStay has been forced by injury to retire.
Di Canio, the former Juventus and AC Milan winger, was fined 25,000 pounds ($41,000) after hinting at a dressing room mutiny as he launched a blistering attack on chief executive McCann.
Di Canio, only 11 months into his four-year contract, accused McCann of "breaking a gentleman's word" in what is believed to be a bonus payment dispute.
But McCann called the accusations "utter nonsense" and immediately fined the Italian and insisted he returns to Scotland from Italy immediately.
In an open letter to Celtic fans, Di Canio said: "The dream I thought I had begun to realise when I became Celtic captain is disintegrating before my eyes.

"I had hoped to lead my team to success but it would go against all my principles if I went on playing for a club whose managing director does not keep the promises he made to me, giving me his gentleman's word, before the start of the season.
"I have had important offers from other clubs but at the moment I do not want to start to consider them because I still hope someone will want to keep me in Glasgow, a city I sincerely love."
Di Canio's sparkling displays and 15 goals have made him an idol with the Celtic fans, whose near 50,000 average support makes them the ninth best-supported club in Europe."

Di Canio is not the first foreign player with whom McCann has had his differences. Portuguese striker Jorge Cadete said the Celtic chief had backed out of a contractual agreement and Dutchman Pierre van Hooydonk, recently sold to Nottingham Forest, made a similar claim.
But McCann hit back, saying: "There is no breach of faith regarding Paolo's contract.
"It is more valuable than any he had at Milan, Juventus or Napoli and has been honoured in every respect. The whole affair is utter nonsense."
And he was unimpressed by Di Canio's claim to "love Glasgow".
"I would think the supporters have heard enough of that" he said.
"This sort of stuff seems to be flavour of the month. Foreign football players all seem to have an angle."

McCann also dismissed Cadete's claim that he had paid 400,000 pounds ($656,000) from his own pocket to Sporting Lisbon to release him from his Celtic contract. "If he has paid that, I should get a refund because Celtic paid every cent of his transfer fee," said McCann.
The row distracted attention from 32-year-old McStay's announcement that a persistent ankle injury had forced his retirement.

McStay, who played 75 times for Scotland and became the second youngest to wear his country's jersey at the age of 18, has been a first team regular at Parkhead since his debut in 1981 as a 17-year-old.
He said on Friday: "The greatest memory I will take away from here was being part of the team which won the championships and Scottish Cup double in 1988.
"I've known for the last week that I would have to quit but I have had to wait this long to compose myself after the shock."
The double dose of bad news is just the latest problem for Celtic in the wake of their failure to halt Rangers' championship dominance in Scotland.

Manager Tommy Burns was sacked last month after their bitter Glasgow rivals won a ninth successive title -- equalling Celtic's record of the 1960s and early 70s -- and after Celtic lost to first division Falkirk in the Cup semifinals.
